title: Time Complexity: Primality
directAnswer: For each query integer, decide 'Prime' or 'Not prime'. The point of the problem is the complexity: test divisibility only up to √n, not n. A number n > 1 is prime iff no integer in [2, √n] divides it — because any factor larger than √n is paired with one smaller than √n. Handle n < 2 as not prime, treat 2 (and 3) as prime, reject even numbers, then trial-divide by odd numbers 3, 5, 7, … while `i·i ≤ n`. Each query is O(√n).

remember.pattern: Trial division up to √n (factors come in pairs straddling √n)
remember.formula:
def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2: return False
    if n < 4: return True           # 2, 3
    if n % 2 == 0: return False
    i = 3
    while i * i <= n:               # only up to sqrt(n)
        if n % i == 0: return False
        i += 2                      # skip evens
    return True
rules: Loop while **`i * i <= n`** (equivalently `i <= sqrt(n)`) — never up to n. That's the whole O(√n) point.
Use `i * i <= n` rather than `i <= sqrt(n)` to **avoid floating-point** rounding errors.
Handle small cases first: `n < 2` → not prime; `2` and `3` are prime.
After ruling out 2, **only test odd divisors** (`i += 2`) — even factors are already covered.
`1` is **not prime**, and neither are `0` or negatives.
whenToUse: Deciding primality of one or a few moderate numbers (up to ~10¹²)
When you need the answer per query, not all primes in a range
Demonstrating the √n factor-pairing insight in an interview
Numbers too large to sieve but small enough for trial division
antiSignals: Many primality tests over a fixed range [1, N] → precompute with a Sieve of Eratosthenes (O(N log log N))
Numbers beyond ~10¹⁸ → need Miller–Rabin probabilistic / deterministic test
You need the factorization, not just prime-or-not → factorize up to √n instead
Counting primes ≤ N → prime-counting / sieve, not per-number trial division
remember.takeaway: Primality by trial division is O(√n) because divisors pair up across √n — find none below √n and there are none at all. The interview signal is choosing √n over n and writing `i*i <= n` to dodge floating-point; for many queries on a bounded range, switch to a sieve.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know that checking divisors only up to √n suffices (and why), and that you write the bound as `i*i <= n` to avoid sqrt rounding — the problem is named after its complexity for a reason.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Looping i up to n (O(n) instead of O(√n)), classifying 1 as prime, or using floating-point `i <= Math.sqrt(n)` and hitting rounding errors near perfect squares.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the factor-pairing argument (a divisor > √n forces a co-divisor < √n), skip even divisors after 2 to halve the work, and mention switching to a sieve when many queries share a bounded range.

problemStatement:
You are given `p` queries; each query is an integer `n`. For each, determine whether `n` is a prime number and print **"Prime"** or **"Not prime"** accordingly.

The task is explicitly about **time complexity**: a naive O(n) check is too slow for large `n`, so you must test primality in **O(√n)** per query.
constraints: Each query must run in O(√n)
1 is not prime; 2 is the smallest prime
Output is exactly "Prime" or "Not prime" per query
understanding: Primality is a yes/no test: n > 1 is prime if it has no divisor other than 1 and itself. The efficiency insight is that divisors come in pairs (d, n/d) that straddle √n, so if no divisor exists at or below √n, none exists above it either. Thus scanning [2, √n] is sufficient and gives O(√n) per query. Special-casing small numbers and skipping evens trims constants.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why is testing up to √n enough?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If n = a·b with a ≤ b, then a ≤ √n. So any composite has a factor at or below √n; finding none there proves primality.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is 1 prime?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. 1 has only one divisor (itself), not two distinct ones, so by definition it is not prime. 0 and negatives are also not prime.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I use Math.sqrt(n) for the bound?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Prefer the integer condition `i*i <= n`. Floating-point sqrt can be slightly off near perfect squares and cause off-by-one errors.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if there are many queries over a fixed range?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then precompute a Sieve of Eratosthenes once in O(N log log N) and answer each query in O(1). Trial division per query is best when n is large and queries are few.

examples.explanation: √5 ≈ 2.23, so we only test i = 3? No — the loop condition 3·3 ≤ 5 is false, so no odd divisor is tested and 5 is declared prime.
1 is excluded by the `n < 2` guard — it is not prime by definition.

diagrams.title: Choosing the right primality method
diagrams.caption: Trial division to √n is the per-query branch; a sieve wins when many queries share a bounded range.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Trial Division up to n−1
approaches.whenToMention: State as the naive version to contrast with √n, since the problem is explicitly about beating O(n).
hints: By definition, n is prime if no integer from 2 to n−1 divides it.
Loop i from 2 to n−1; if any i divides n evenly, n is composite.
If the loop finishes with no divisor, n is prime. This is correct but O(n) — too slow for n up to 2×10⁹.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The loop runs up to n−2 iterations in the worst case (a prime), each an O(1) modulo, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
The literal definition: a prime has no divisors strictly between 1 and itself, so test them all.

**The loop.** For each `i` from 2 to `n − 1`, check `n % i == 0`. The first such `i` proves `n` composite; reaching the end proves it prime. Guard `n < 2` as not prime up front.

**Why it's correct but unacceptable here.** For a prime `n = 2×10⁹` this performs ~2 billion modulo operations per query — far too slow within typical limits, and the problem name *Time Complexity: Primality* is a direct hint that O(n) is the wrong answer. We show it only to motivate the √n cutoff: most of those iterations are wasted because divisors past √n are redundant.
approaches.insight: Every iteration past √n only finds the larger half of a factor pair you'd already have caught below √n — so half the search space is pure redundancy. That observation is exactly what the optimal version removes.

dryRun.intro: Test every i from 2 upward until a divisor appears.

java.line: for (long i = 2; i < n; i++) {        // up to n-1 — O(n)
java.explanation: Tests every candidate divisor — far more than necessary.
Any exact divisor proves n composite.

python.line: for i in range(2, n):                 # up to n-1 — O(n)
python.explanation: The naive full scan — too slow for large n.

diagrams.title: Why the upper half is wasted
diagrams.caption: Divisors pair across √n; anything found above it was already findable below.

pitfalls: Running to n−1 — O(n) is too slow for n up to 2×10⁹.
Treating 1 as prime by omitting the n < 2 guard.
Starting the loop at 1 — 1 divides everything, falsely marking all numbers composite.

approaches.name: Trial Division up to √n, Skipping Evens (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The expected answer. Phrase it as 'a composite must have a factor ≤ √n, so I only test up to √n, odds only'.
hints: If n = a·b with a ≤ b then a ≤ √n, so any composite has a divisor at or below √n. Testing [2, √n] is sufficient.
Write the loop bound as `i*i <= n` rather than `i <= sqrt(n)` to avoid floating-point rounding near perfect squares.
Handle n < 2 (not prime), 2 and 3 (prime), and even n (not prime) first; then test only odd i = 3, 5, 7, … incrementing by 2.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The loop runs while `i*i <= n` over odd i, i.e. about √n / 2 iterations, each an O(1) modulo → O(√n) time, O(1) space. The even-skip halves the constant.
approaches.explanation:
Cut the search at √n and skip the evens.

**The √n cutoff.** Suppose `n` is composite, `n = a·b` with `a ≤ b`. Then `a·a ≤ a·b = n`, so `a ≤ √n`. Every composite therefore has a divisor at or below √n. Contrapositive: if nothing in `[2, √n]` divides `n`, then `n` has no nontrivial divisor at all and is prime. That single fact turns the O(n) scan into O(√n).

**Integer bound, not floating-point.** Write the condition as `i*i <= n`. Using `i <= Math.sqrt(n)` invites trouble: `sqrt` returns a double that can be marginally below the true root for a perfect square (e.g. `sqrt(n)` computed as `…9999`), causing the loop to stop one short and misclassify `n`. The integer product comparison is exact.

**Skip evens.** After confirming `n` isn't even (and handling 2 itself as prime), no even number can be a factor, so we only need odd candidates: start `i = 3` and step by 2. This halves the iterations.

**Small-number guards.** `n < 2` → not prime. `n < 4` (i.e. 2 or 3) → prime, which also lets the odd loop start cleanly at 3 without a special first iteration. `n % 2 == 0` (and n ≥ 4) → not prime.

**Per-query cost.** Each query is O(√n) ≈ 45,000 modulo operations for `n = 2×10⁹` — trivially fast, and well within limits for up to 30 queries.
approaches.insight: Factor pairing `(d, n/d)` reflecting across √n is the whole idea: search only the smaller half. Combined with the `i*i <= n` integer test (no floating-point) and the odd-only step, it's the clean, bug-free primality check interviewers expect.

dryRun.intro: Guards pass (29 ≥ 4, odd). Test odd i while i*i ≤ 29; √29 ≈ 5.39 so we test 3 and 5.

java.line: if (n < 4) return true;               // 2 and 3 are prime
java.explanation: Handles the only primes below the odd loop's starting point.

java.line: if (n % 2 == 0) return false;         // drop all evens > 2
java.explanation: Removes every even composite so the loop can step by 2.

java.line: for (long i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) {// odd divisors up to sqrt(n)
java.explanation: Integer bound `i*i <= n` avoids floating-point sqrt errors; odds only.
A divisor at or below √n proves n composite.

python.line:
if n < 4:
        return True                       # 2 and 3 are prime
python.explanation: Small primes handled before the loop.

python.line:
if n % 2 == 0:
        return False                      # drop all evens > 2
python.explanation: Even numbers above 2 are never prime.

python.line: while i * i <= n:                      # odd divisors up to sqrt(n)
python.explanation: Exact integer cutoff at √n — the source of O(√n).
Step over even candidates; only odd divisors remain to test.

diagrams.title: Decision flow
diagrams.caption: Guards short-circuit small and even cases; the loop only tests odd i up to √n.

edgeCases.behavior: n < 4 → returns true. The smallest and only even prime.
n < 2 → returns false. 1 is not prime.
Odd, i=3: 3·3=9 ≤ 9 and 9 % 3 == 0 → Not prime. The perfect square that `i*i <= n` catches exactly where floating-point might fail.

pitfalls: Using `i <= Math.sqrt(n)` — floating-point rounding can misclassify perfect squares like 9, 25, 49.
Forgetting to special-case 2 while skipping evens — would wrongly mark 2 as composite or start the loop wrong.
Off-by-one with `i < i*i` style conditions — use `i*i <= n` so the divisor equal to √n is tested.

commonMistakes: Looping divisors up to n instead of √n — O(n) is too slow for large inputs.
Using floating-point Math.sqrt for the bound and misclassifying perfect squares.
Classifying 1 (or 0/negatives) as prime by omitting the n < 2 guard.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Scanning to n instead of √n
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The factor-pairing argument shows divisors above √n are redundant. Looping to n is O(n) and times out for n up to 2×10⁹.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Floating-point sqrt bound
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Math.sqrt returns a double that may be slightly below the true root for perfect squares, stopping the loop one short and misclassifying n.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: for (long i = 3; i <= Math.sqrt(n); i += 2) { ... }  // rounding risk
commonMistakesDetailed.good: for (long i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) { ... }          // exact integer test

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating 1 as prime
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 1 has no second distinct divisor, so it is not prime. Without the `n < 2` guard it slips through the loop (which never executes) and is wrongly reported prime.

patternNote: Trial-division primality is O(√n) because a composite's factors pair across √n — test only the smaller half. Write the bound as `i*i <= n` to stay in integer arithmetic, and skip evens to halve the constant. For many queries over a fixed range, precompute with a sieve instead.
